blocks.content: Every time a database looks up a row by its primary key, it needs to find that row among potentially billions of others, fast, and it needs to do it while most of that data lives on disk, not in memory. A B-Tree, and its close relative the B+ Tree, is the data structure nearly every relational database has relied on for this exact job since the 1970s, precisely because it was designed from the ground up around the one constraint that matters most here: disk access is slow, and memory access is fast.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283478684-987409843.png
blocks.alt: A single disk access can take a million times longer than a single memory access, a gap so large it shapes the entire design of database indexes

blocks.content: 1. Why Databases Need a Special Data Structure At All
blocks.text: 1. Why Databases Need a Special Data Structure At All

blocks.content: A regular binary search tree seems like the obvious choice for keeping sorted data searchable, it gives you logarithmic search time, which sounds great on paper. The problem is not the algorithm, it is where the data actually lives. A production database table can hold hundreds of millions of rows, far more than fits in memory, which means most of the tree has to live on disk.

And disk access is not just a little slower than memory access, it is dramatically slower, often by a factor of 100,000 or more when comparing a solid-state drive read to a memory read, and the gap is even larger against a traditional spinning disk. Every single node visited during a search that lives on disk costs a disk seek, and a data structure optimized purely for algorithmic elegance, ignoring where its nodes physically live, quickly becomes a performance disaster at real scale.

This is not a minor implementation detail either, it is the single most important fact shaping how every serious storage engine is built. A data structure that ignores this gap and optimizes purely for the number of comparisons made, the classic measure of algorithmic efficiency in a computer science course, can end up dramatically slower in the real world than one that minimizes disk seeks instead, even if it needs more total comparisons to do so.
2. The Problem with a Plain Binary Search Tree on Disk
blocks.text: 2. The Problem with a Plain Binary Search Tree on Disk

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396029482-962750644.png
blocks.alt: A binary tree with only two children per node has to be very deep to hold millions of rows, and every level of depth is another disk seek

blocks.content: A binary search tree holding one million rows needs roughly 20 levels of depth, since each node only branches into two children. If each level lives on a different disk page, a single lookup could mean 20 separate disk seeks, and at millisecond-scale seek times, that adds up to a genuinely slow query, one users would notice.

The fundamental issue is the branching factor, how many children each node has. A binary tree is stuck at two, no matter how it is tuned. Fixing this cheap disk-seek problem means fundamentally rethinking how many children a single node can have.

It is worth noting this problem exists independent of how well the binary tree happens to be balanced, even a perfectly balanced binary tree still only branches twice per node, the depth problem is structural, not a symptom of poor balancing that a smarter balancing algorithm could fix on its own.
3. What a B-Tree Actually Is
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283482619-634642423.png
blocks.alt: A B-Tree node holds hundreds of keys at once, so the same amount of data fits in a tree only a few levels deep

blocks.content: A B-Tree solves the branching factor problem directly: instead of two children per node, a single B-Tree node holds many keys at once, often hundreds, and branches into just as many children. The same million rows that needed 20 levels in a binary tree might fit in a B-Tree only 3 or 4 levels deep, turning 20 potential disk seeks into 3 or 4.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283484338-716860508.png
blocks.alt: Each node stores a sorted list of keys alongside pointers to the child nodes that fall between them

blocks.content: Each node stores its keys in sorted order, along with pointers to child nodes, where each child holds keys that fall in the range between two consecutive keys in the parent. This keeps the entire structure searchable with a simple, repeated binary search within each node, followed by a jump to the appropriate child.
3.1 Searching within a single node
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283486045-661220162.png
blocks.alt: Finding the right key inside one wide node still uses ordinary binary search, since the keys within a node are kept sorted

blocks.content: It is worth being precise that a B-Tree is not really replacing binary search, it is nesting it. Within a single node holding, say, 200 sorted keys, finding the right position still uses a normal binary search, comparing against roughly 8 keys to narrow down to the correct child pointer. The real innovation is doing this once per node, across only 3 or 4 nodes total, rather than once per level across 20 separate nodes.

It is worth being precise that keys within a node act purely as dividers, the pointer between two keys leads to a subtree containing every value that falls between them, which is exactly what makes the structure a natural fit for sorted, ordered data rather than an unordered collection.

The name itself, incidentally, does not stand for anything universally agreed upon, Bayer, balanced, and broad have all been suggested as the origin of the B, and even its original inventors have been coy about the exact meaning, a fun bit of trivia that rarely comes up but is occasionally asked.
4. Why Wide and Shallow Beats Tall and Narrow
blocks.text: 4. Why Wide and Shallow Beats Tall and Narrow

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283487766-412575658.png
blocks.alt: A higher fanout, more keys per node, means a shallower tree overall, and a shallower tree means fewer disk reads for any given lookup

blocks.content: This "wide and shallow instead of tall and narrow" shape is the entire point. The number of children a node can have is called its fanout, and a database tunes the fanout specifically to match the size of one disk page, typically 4 or 8 kilobytes, packing as many keys as possible into each node so that reading one node means reading exactly one disk page, no more, no less.
4.1 A concrete sense of scale

With a fanout of around 200 keys per node, a B+ Tree can hold 200 entries at depth 1, 40,000 at depth 2, 8 million at depth 3, and 1.6 billion at just depth 4. That last number is worth sitting with, a table with over a billion rows can still be searched in roughly 4 disk reads, an almost unbelievable ratio once you actually see the numbers laid out.

These numbers assume a fanout tuned to match a typical disk page size, actual values vary by database engine and configuration, but the underlying shape, an extra level of depth buying an enormous jump in capacity, holds true across nearly every real B+ Tree implementation in production use today.
5. Node Structure and Splitting

A B-Tree keeps itself balanced automatically through a rule enforced on every insertion: every node must stay within a defined minimum and maximum number of keys. Insert enough keys into a node to push it past its maximum, and the node splits.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283489538-894811171.png
blocks.alt: When a node fills up, it splits into two nodes, and the middle key gets promoted up into the parent to keep everything searchable

blocks.content: Splitting works by dividing the overfull node roughly in half, and promoting its middle key up into the parent node to act as the new dividing line between the two resulting children. If that promotion causes the parent itself to overflow, the same splitting process cascades upward, which is how a B-Tree grows in height only from the root, keeping itself balanced without ever needing a separate rebalancing pass.

A well-tuned B-Tree keeps nodes at least half full at all times as a design invariant, which bounds how much wasted space the structure can accumulate, and guarantees the worst-case tree height stays close to the best-case height, an important property for predictable performance under real, messy insert and delete patterns rather than only under a carefully constructed benchmark.
5.1 Merging on deletion, the mirror of splitting
blocks.text: 5.1 Merging on deletion, the mirror of splitting

blocks.content: Deletion works in the opposite direction. Removing a key can leave a node under its required minimum, in which case it either borrows a key from an adjacent sibling node, or, if the sibling has no spare keys to lend, merges entirely with that sibling. Just like splitting, a merge can cascade upward if it leaves the parent under its own minimum, keeping the tree balanced in both directions, growth and shrinkage alike.
6. B+ Trees: The Difference That Actually Matters
blocks.text: 6. B+ Trees: The Difference That Actually Matters

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283491237-320109471.png
blocks.alt: In a B+ Tree, only the leaf nodes hold the actual data; internal nodes exist purely to route a search toward the right leaf

blocks.content: A B+ Tree is a specific variation almost every real database actually uses, rather than a plain B-Tree. The difference: in a B+ Tree, only the leaf nodes store actual data, every internal node exists purely as a routing structure, holding copies of keys just to direct a search toward the correct leaf, never the data itself.

The second defining feature is that every leaf node is linked to its neighboring leaf, left and right, forming an ordered chain across the very bottom of the tree. This one addition is what makes B+ Trees dramatically better suited to how databases actually get queried.
6.1 A small cost for a large benefit
blocks.text: 6.1 A small cost for a large benefit

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283493356-660731210.png
blocks.alt: A single point lookup in a B+ Tree does one extra hop compared to a plain B-Tree, since even a direct key match still has to walk down to a leaf

blocks.content: This design is not entirely free. A single-key lookup in a plain B-Tree can sometimes find its answer at an internal node partway down the tree, if that key happens to live there. A B+ Tree always walks all the way down to a leaf, even for a single key match, since that is the only place data actually lives. In practice this costs at most one extra level of traversal, a small, predictable price for the much larger benefit range queries get in return.

Some real-world implementations optimize around even this small cost, keeping a small amount of the most frequently accessed data cached separately in memory, so the extra hop to a leaf rarely translates into an extra real disk read in practice, only an extra pointer traversal within data already resident in memory.
7. Why Databases Prefer B+ Trees Specifically
blocks.text: 7. Why Databases Prefer B+ Trees Specifically

blocks.content: Keeping data only in the leaves means internal nodes can be smaller (since they hold routing keys, not full records) and therefore pack a higher fanout into a single disk page, an even shallower tree than a plain B-Tree achieves for the same data.

There is a second, related benefit worth naming directly: keeping all data at a single, uniform depth (every leaf) makes the cost of any lookup far more predictable than in a plain B-Tree, where a lucky search might terminate early at an internal node while an unlucky one goes all the way down. Predictable, uniform latency is often just as valuable to a database as raw average speed, especially for the tail latency a production system actually gets measured on.

Taken together, these two advantages, higher fanout from smaller internal nodes and fast ordered range access from linked leaves, explain why B+ Trees became the near-universal default rather than just one option among several equally common choices.
8. Range Queries and Why B+ Trees Excel at Them
blocks.text: 8. Range Queries and Why B+ Trees Excel at Them

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396030016-766525835.png
blocks.alt: Finding the start of a range and then simply walking the linked leaves forward makes range queries fast and simple

blocks.content: This is where the linked-leaves design truly pays off. A query like "find every order placed between January 1st and January 31st" needs a range query, not a single lookup. With linked leaves, the database finds the starting key once, then simply walks forward along the leaf chain, collecting every subsequent value in order, until it passes the end of the range.

-- a range query that benefits directly from B+ Tree leaf linking
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-01-31'
ORDER BY created_at;

code.content:
-- a range query that benefits directly from B+ Tree leaf linking
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-01-31'
ORDER BY created_at;

codes.sql:
-- a range query that benefits directly from B+ Tree leaf linking
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-01-31'
ORDER BY created_at;

blocks.content: A plain B-Tree, where data can live at any level, would need to repeatedly traverse back up and down the tree to collect an ordered range, meaningfully more work than simply walking a flat, linked chain of leaves.

blocks.title: Why this matters beyond a single query
blocks.content: Range scans are not a rare, special case, ORDER BY, BETWEEN, pagination, and most reporting queries all rely on efficiently reading a sorted range of rows, which is exactly why nearly every relational database defaults to B+ Trees rather than a plain B-Tree.

Pagination is a particularly common, everyday example of this exact benefit at work, fetching page after page of sorted results is, under the hood, simply continuing to walk the same linked leaf chain from wherever the previous page left off, rather than repeating a full search from the root each time.
9. Insertion and the Splitting Process in Practice
blocks.text: 9. Insertion and the Splitting Process in Practice

blocks.content: Inserting a new key always starts by searching down to the correct leaf, the same way a lookup would, and inserting the key there in sorted order. Only if that leaf is now over capacity does a split actually happen, keeping the common case, inserting into a leaf with room to spare, cheap and fast.

Because splits happen only occasionally, most insertions are genuinely cheap, a single leaf write plus updating one internal pointer, which is why B+ Trees remain a solid choice even for write-heavy workloads, though LSM Trees, covered separately in this section, push write throughput further still by taking a fundamentally different approach.

Deletions in practice are handled somewhat conservatively by many real database engines, some choose to tolerate temporarily under-full nodes rather than aggressively merging on every single delete, trading a small amount of wasted space for avoiding unnecessary restructuring work on a hot write path.
10. Real-World Usage

{"headers":["Database","How it uses B+ Trees"],"rows":[["MySQL (InnoDB)","The primary key index is a B+ Tree with the actual row data stored directly in the leaves"],["PostgreSQL","B+ Trees back the default index type for most columns"],["SQLite","Uses B+ Trees for both table storage and secondary indexes"]]}

It is worth knowing that InnoDB specifically stores the actual row data directly inside the primary key B+ Tree leaves, called a clustered index, while a secondary index B+ Tree stores the primary key value in its leaves instead of the full row, requiring one extra lookup into the primary tree to fetch the complete row, a detail that explains why queries on secondary indexes are sometimes noticeably slower than primary key lookups.
10.1 Secondary indexes are separate trees entirely
blocks.text: 10.1 Secondary indexes are separate trees entirely

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785283496857-37050626.png
blocks.alt: Every additional index on a table is its own independent B+ Tree, maintained alongside the primary key tree

blocks.content: It is a common point of confusion that a table has "one index." In reality, the primary key gets its own B+ Tree, and every additional column indexed (an email address, a timestamp) gets its own separate B+ Tree too, each one fully maintained, split, and rebalanced independently on every write that touches an indexed column. This is exactly why adding indexes carelessly has a real, compounding cost on write performance, each one is genuinely a whole extra tree to keep up to date.

This is a large part of why schema design advice so often includes limiting indexes to columns actually used in WHERE clauses, JOIN conditions, or ORDER BY, rather than indexing defensively, every unused index is pure write overhead with no corresponding read benefit to justify it.
11. Common Mistakes

["Assuming a B-Tree and a B+ Tree are the same thing, and missing the leaf-linking detail that actually explains why range queries are fast.","Forgetting that every additional secondary index is its own separate B+ Tree, with its own real storage and maintenance cost on every write.","Assuming a B-Tree index always helps, a query pattern that never does range scans or sorted access can sometimes be served just as well, or better, by a simpler structure."]
items: Assuming a B-Tree and a B+ Tree are the same thing, and missing the leaf-linking detail that actually explains why range queries are fast.
Forgetting that every additional secondary index is its own separate B+ Tree, with its own real storage and maintenance cost on every write.
Assuming a B-Tree index always helps, a query pattern that never does range scans or sorted access can sometimes be served just as well, or better, by a simpler structure.

blocks.content: ["Choosing a very large number of small, narrow secondary indexes without considering their combined write overhead.","Assuming an index automatically speeds up every query touching that column, when in fact the query planner may reasonably decide a full table scan is actually cheaper for a low-selectivity column."]
items: Choosing a very large number of small, narrow secondary indexes without considering their combined write overhead.
Assuming an index automatically speeds up every query touching that column, when in fact the query planner may reasonably decide a full table scan is actually cheaper for a low-selectivity column.

blocks.content: A further mistake worth naming is indexing a column with very low cardinality, like a boolean flag with only two possible values, where a B+ Tree index rarely helps the query planner narrow anything down meaningfully, while still paying the full maintenance cost of keeping that index updated on every write.
12. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 12. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: Strong answers explain the disk-versus-memory latency gap as the actual motivation before describing the structure itself, since that gap is why this data structure looks the way it does. Knowing the specific difference between a B-Tree and a B+ Tree, data only in the leaves, leaves linked together, and being able to connect that directly to why range queries are fast, shows real depth beyond simply naming the structure.
A B+ Tree is not a cleverer algorithm than a binary search tree, it is the same idea reshaped around one hard constraint: disk seeks are expensive, so touch as few pages as possible.

A good follow-up to be ready for is comparing this structure directly against a hash index, a hash index can be faster for pure equality lookups but offers no help at all for range queries or sorted access, which is exactly the gap a B+ Tree is built to fill, and why databases typically offer both index types rather than picking just one.

Being able to sketch a small B+ Tree by hand, showing a split happening as new keys are added, is often the single most convincing way to demonstrate real understanding of this structure in an interview setting, far more so than reciting its properties from memory.
Key Takeaways

["B-Trees and B+ Trees exist because disk access is dramatically slower than memory access, making a wide, shallow tree far better than a tall, narrow one.","A high fanout, many keys per node, keeps the tree shallow enough that a lookup touches only a handful of disk pages.","Nodes split automatically when they overflow, keeping the tree balanced without a separate rebalancing pass.","A B+ Tree keeps data only in its leaf nodes, and links those leaves together, which is what makes range queries fast.","Nearly every major relational database (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite) uses B+ Trees as its default index structure."]
items: B-Trees and B+ Trees exist because disk access is dramatically slower than memory access, making a wide, shallow tree far better than a tall, narrow one.
A high fanout, many keys per node, keeps the tree shallow enough that a lookup touches only a handful of disk pages.
Nodes split automatically when they overflow, keeping the tree balanced without a separate rebalancing pass.
A B+ Tree keeps data only in its leaf nodes, and links those leaves together, which is what makes range queries fast.
Nearly every major relational database (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite) uses B+ Trees as its default index structure.

blocks.content: Read this topic alongside LSM Trees in this same section for the fuller picture, B+ Trees and LSM Trees represent two genuinely different philosophies for the exact same underlying problem, and understanding why a real system might choose one over the other is one of the more revealing questions in this entire area of system design.

Once this structure clicks, a lot of otherwise mysterious database behavior starts to make sense, why adding an index speeds up some queries and not others, why a schema migration on a huge table can take a while, and why a sorted, ranged query so often outperforms an equivalent unsorted scan by a wide margin.
